title: Ammonite shell and aptychus are two parts of a once united split cone

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Ammonite shell and aptychus are two parts of a once united split cone

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The shell and the aptychus of ammonites are probably the ventral and dorsal portions of a once united conical shell split by unequal growth, as in pteropods; other cephalopods retain only one of the two, the ventral one as the shell of Nautilus and the dorsal one as the shell of Sepia or Spirula.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In short, I think there is reason to believe, or at least to suspect, that we have in the shell and Aptychus of the Ammonites, two portions of a once united structure; of which other Cephalopods retain not both parts but only one or other, one as the ventrally situated shell of Nautilus, the other as the dorsally placed shell for example of Sepia or of Spirula.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XI, “The Logarithmic Spiral”; topic “Pteropod shells and cephalopod shells”. Scope: ammonoids, Nautilus, Sepia, Spirula and other cephalopods; thecosome pteropods

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch11-19: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.53

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern fossil and comparative data can test several consequences and likely reject or support homology hypotheses. The exact ancestral split event is a historical inference with incomplete preservation, preventing full resolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Combine fossil positional evidence, microstructure and independent cephalopod phylogenies to test homology between ammonite aptychi and dorsal shell components, and compare developmental boundary predictions from a split-cone model. Support requires congruent tissue homology and ancestral-state reconstruction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Deep homology alternatives can fit fragmentary fossil evidence.

Soft-tissue attachment and embryonic stages are rarely preserved.

The once-united ancestral structure is not directly observable.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Specimens and images of aptychi, ammonoid shells and the living analogues exist in open collections, so microstructure and position can be compared for a subset. Thompson frames the idea as a suspicion, and several homology schemes remain compatible with the same fossils. The data can damage or mildly support the split-cone reading and cannot reconstruct the unobserved united shell.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare aptychus microstructure, growth and position with ammonoid shells, Nautilus, Sepia, Spirula and thecosome pteropods under explicit homology criteria for a split cone. Shared growth and shell microstructure would support the united-cone hypothesis; jaw- or operculum-like structure and a mismatch with Sepia or Spirula would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ammonites provide no developmental series that could show a cone splitting into shell and aptychus.

Homology criteria for extinct hard parts are contested, so the same specimens can be scored for more than one identification.
